svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Three types of natural selection acting on a continuous trait."], [1, "Stabilising: the extremes do worse; the distribution narrows around the same mean."], [5, "Directional: one extreme does better; the whole distribution shifts."], [9, "Disruptive: both extremes do better; the distribution splits into two peaks."]]
svg.title: Types of natural selection
svg.desc: Stabilising, directional and disruptive selection shown as changing frequency distributions of a heritable trait, before and after selection, with examples.
svg.text: Dashed curve = original population; solid = after several generations.

g.data-info: The intermediate phenotype is favoured and both extremes are selected against: the mean stays the same and variation decreases. Example: human birth mass.
One extreme is favoured: the mean shifts in that direction. Examples: antibiotic resistance, dark peppered moths in polluted areas.
Both extremes are favoured over the intermediate: the population may split into two peaks, which can lead to speciation. Example: large and small beaks in black-bellied seedcrackers.
Number of individuals against a heritable trait. Dashed: before selection. Solid: after selection. Red arrows: individuals selected against.
g.text: y-axis: number of individuals · x-axis: value of a heritable trait (e.g. mass, beak depth)
Selection acts on phenotypes; allele frequencies change in the next generations.
